list.line: Gel your hands, greet with name and role, check name and date of birth, agree why you are here.
list.why: You do this in every station, so it should run as a routine, like a footballer's run-up. A 4-beat rhythm triggers it faster than letters.
list.no: No acronym: under stress you would waste a second decoding letters for something your hands already know.

list.code: Sum it · Check it · Net it · Thank them
list.line: Summarise the plan, check understanding, safety-net (what, who, how fast), thank them and gel.
list.why: Four short verbs in the order you say them. The safety-net is the mark most often dropped at 9:30, and the rhythm keeps it in.
list.no: Keep it to 4 beats; anything longer gets cut when the bell is about to go.

list.why: Three letters that examiners literally tick. A tiny fixed set is exactly what letter mnemonics are good at.
list.no: Ask it as a conversation, not a checklist ("Is there anything you were worried this might be?").
L: Ideas: what do you think is going on?
Expectations: what were you hoping we would do today?
Impact: how is it affecting work, sleep, family?

list.why: Five questions in the order an examiner thinks. Each W is a question, so it can't be decoded wrong the way a letter can.
list.no: Don't recite the whole history back; the 5 Ws force you to choose.
L: Age, setting, main problem in one line
The clue that clinches your diagnosis
The dangerous alternative and how you would exclude it
Bedside, bloods, imaging, then first management

list.why: A fixed set of 8 that every examiner knows, in a natural order. Letters work well for this.
list.no: Only for pain. For breathlessness, diarrhoea or a lump use onset, duration, pattern, better or worse, impact. Forcing SOCRATES onto them sounds robotic.

list.why: A screen of 9 items with no natural order: the kind of list letters handle best.
list.no: In a focused 10-minute station, ask the 2 or 3 that matter for this complaint plus "anything else you see a doctor for?". Reading all 9 costs a minute.

list.why: Five quick items you ask every time; letters stop you forgetting driving and work, which carry the hidden marks (DVLA, occupational exposure).
list.no: Count, don't judge: "How many units a week?" with no comment.
L: Who is at home, and how they manage

list.line: Prescribed, bought over the counter, herbal, then allergies with what actually happened.
list.why: One chain in the order you ask it. Asking what the reaction was separates a true allergy (rash, swelling, breathing) from an intolerance (nausea).
list.no: Never write "allergy: penicillin" without the reaction; that's the mark.

list.why: "Prescribe energy capsules": a picture phrase that unpacks into 8 symptoms. Letters suit a fixed symptom set.
list.no: Ask low mood and anhedonia first (the 2 core questions), then the rest. Don't interrogate in letter order if they start talking.

list.t: Mania screen (ask even when it looks like depression)
list.why: Missing bipolar changes treatment (antidepressants alone can trigger mania), so a fixed screen earns the differential mark.
list.no: One question covers most of it: "Have you ever had times you felt so high or full of energy that others worried?"

list.code: Risk ladder: climb, look back, look around
list.why: The ladder goes up in severity, so you naturally stop and act when they are high on it. Grouping beats a 6-letter code here.
list.no: NICE (NG225) says don't use risk scores to predict suicide. Use the ladder to understand the person, then agree a safety plan.
L: Thoughts → plans → intent → means → preparation (note, saving tablets, goodbyes)
Past attempts and self-harm: how lethal, what stopped them
Protective factors, who is at home, children, access to means
Risk to others, from others, and self-neglect

list.why: A fixed 7-part order that examiners expect to hear, so letters suit it. The word itself prompts "clean, ordered" presenting.
list.no: Add Risk at the end; ASEPTIC leaves it out and it's the mark people lose.
L: Emotion: mood (their words) and affect (what you see)

list.code: Mood is the climate, affect is the weather
list.line: Mood = how they say they have felt over weeks (climate). Affect = what you observe moment to moment (weather).
list.why: One contrast you must not mix up. A picture comparison sticks better than definitions.
list.no: Gemini had this backwards ("mood = weather"). Weather changes by the minute, like affect.

list.line: Ask what they know, tell one small chunk in plain words, ask what they took from it. Repeat.
list.why: This loop is chunk-and-check plus teach-back, which are both explicit marks. A 3-beat loop is easier to run live than a 10-item list.
list.no: If the examiner can't hear you checking understanding, you lose the mark. Say it out loud.

list.why: Your fixed counselling sequence (from your formative feedback) packed into 4 groups that fit 10 minutes.
list.no: Don't read the BNF or leaflet aloud; check one fact if you have to.
L: The condition and how the drug helps (one sentence on mechanism)
Dose, time of day, with or without food, how long, missed dose
Common side effects; serious ones and what to do now; interactions, alcohol, driving, pregnancy

list.why: The order matters (perception before knowledge), and the acronym holds it.
list.no: The marks are in the warning shot and the silence afterwards. Don't rush K to get to S.
L: Setting: private, sit down, support person
Perception: what do you already know?
Invitation: how much would you like to know?
Knowledge: warning shot, then the news in plain words
Strategy and summary: next steps, who and when

list.t: Error, complaint or duty of candour
list.line: Say sorry for the error itself, say what happened (facts only), what we have done now, what happens next (report, review), and who can help (PALS, complaint).
list.why: Five short beats that follow how an upset person needs information. "Sorry" is not an admission of liability.
list.no: No acronym; the mark is a sincere apology in plain words, not a code.

list.why: De-escalation is a sequence; doing it in order stops you defending before listening.
list.no: Don't blame colleagues or guess at causes; stick to facts.

list.line: Stage 1: is there an impairment of mind or brain? Stage 2: can they understand, retain, use and weigh, and communicate the decision?
list.why: The statutory words are the mark, so learn them as they are. It is decision-specific and you start by assuming capacity.
list.no: Don't turn it into letters: "URWC" adds a decoding step and nothing else.

list.why: The NHS standard, so the person receiving it expects this order.
list.no: Lead with the concern in the first sentence; don't save it for R.
L: Situation: who you are, who the patient is, the problem, your concern
Recommendation: exactly what you want and by when

list.code: "Out of 100 people like you, over 10 years…"
list.line: Absolute numbers, same denominator, same time frame, for benefit and harm.
list.why: People understand natural frequencies far better than percentages or relative risk. A ready-made sentence means you can't slip into "halves your risk".
list.no: Never give relative risk alone.

list.why: Order by what kills first. Letters suit it because the order is fixed and universal.
list.no: Treat as you find, then reassess. Don't finish all letters before acting.
L: Circulation: HR, BP, CRT, IV access, bloods, fluids
Disability: ACVPU or GCS, pupils, glucose

list.line: Most patients 94 to 98%; at risk of hypercapnia (COPD, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular) 88 to 92%.
list.why: Two numbers that decide the prescription; numbers stick when paired with the condition that changes them.
list.no: Critically ill patients get high-flow oxygen first, then titrate.

list.why: Five questions every prescription must answer, grouped the way you read the chart from left to right.
list.no: Check kidney and liver function and interactions before "What"; the chunks don't replace thinking.
L: Patient details, weight, allergies and reactions
Dose with units (micrograms in full), route, frequency
Start date, review or stop date, indication

list.code: Rate · Rhythm · Axis · then P to T
list.why: Same order every time, so you never jump to the eye-catching ST change and miss the AF.
list.no: Always state patient details and the date first; the system starts after that.
L: P waves, PR, QRS width, ST, T waves, QT

list.why: A fixed route through the film; letters stop you skipping the review areas where the hidden finding sits.
list.no: If a big finding jumps out, say it first, then go systematic.
L: Details: name, date, PA or AP
RIPE quality: rotation, inspiration, projection, exposure
Everything else: bones, lines, tubes, review areas

list.why: Five fixed opening marks; letters make sure none is skipped.
list.no: It should take 30 seconds. Don't perform it slowly to show off.
L: Introduce and identify (name, date of birth)

list.code: End of bed → hands → face → neck → organ → legs → complete
list.why: Your hands travel up and back down the body, so the body itself cues the next stop. Route memory (method of loci) gave a medium-sized boost to recall in a 2021 meta-analysis.
list.no: No letters needed: the patient in front of you is the mnemonic.
L: End of the bed: patient and surroundings
The organ: inspect, palpate, percuss, auscultate

list.why: Four steps in a fixed order.
list.no: Neuro and joints use different spines (tone, power… and look, feel, move). Don't force IPPA onto them.

list.why: A sentence for 4 places in order across the chest. You listen in the order you say it.
list.no: Then do the manoeuvres: left lateral (mitral stenosis, bell at apex), sit forward on breath out (aortic regurgitation).

list.code: MS lies left, AR leans forward
list.line: Mitral stenosis: roll to the left, bell at the apex. Aortic regurgitation: sit forward, breathe out, diaphragm at the left sternal edge.
list.why: A body position you can picture beats a list.
list.no: Say the manoeuvre aloud even if you hear nothing.

list.code: Fluid and air push; collapse and scar pull
list.line: Away from a large effusion or tension pneumothorax; towards collapse, fibrosis or pneumonectomy.
list.why: One contrast that settles the respiratory diagnosis.
list.no: A central trachea doesn't exclude a small effusion.

list.why: Five verbs in the order your hands use them, done twice (front, then back).
list.no: Compare side to side at every level; that comparison is the mark.

list.why: The alphabet is a list you already know perfectly, so it carries 10 signs for free.
list.no: Say them as you reach each body part (hands, then face, then chest), not as a recited list.

list.line: Lie flat with one pillow, start furthest from the pain, and watch their face, not your hands.
list.why: Three safety marks in three words.
list.no: Kneel to the bed's level; it shows you are looking at their face.

list.code: Below the belt, then the dip
list.why: Groups the "to complete" list by body region, so you sweep downwards and finish at the urine pot.
list.no: Say it; don't do it. These are offered, not performed, in the station.
L: Urine dip (and pregnancy test where relevant)

list.why: Five tests on one nerve, held in a short word.
list.no: Then move down the face for the other nerves; the route is your cue for the rest.

list.why: You move down the head in the same order the nerves appear. That beats a numbered list.
list.no: The "Some Say Marry Money…" rhyme tells you sensory or motor, not the order of testing. Keep the two separate.

list.code: Weber: conductive goes to the bad ear
list.line: Rinne positive (air louder than bone) is normal. Weber goes to the bad ear in conductive loss and the good ear in sensorineural loss.
list.why: One rule settles the hearing-loss type.
list.no: Use a 512 Hz fork, not 128 Hz.

list.code: I · T · P · R · C · S
list.why: Six steps in a fixed order that never changes between arms and legs.
list.no: Compare sides at each step; do sensation distal to proximal.
L: Inspect (and pronator drift in the arms)
Sensation: light touch, pin-prick, vibration, proprioception

list.code: 1-2 buckle my shoe, 3-4 kick the door, 5-6 pick up sticks, 7-8 lay them straight
list.line: Ankle S1–2, knee L3–4, biceps and supinator C5–6, triceps C7–8.
list.why: A nursery rhyme you already know, matched to an action of each reflex. Rhyme is retrieved without decoding.
list.no: Root values are for presenting, not the order you test in.

list.why: Six signs with no natural order, so letters do the work.
list.no: Signs are on the same side as the lesion. Say that when you present.

list.code: Swallow moves the gland, tongue moves the cyst
list.line: A goitre rises on swallowing; a thyroglossal cyst rises when the tongue sticks out.
list.why: One contrast that answers "what is this lump?".
list.no: Ask them to swallow water and to stick their tongue out every time, even if you think you know.

list.code: Lid lag: any; bulging and shins: Graves' only
list.line: Lid lag and lid retraction happen in any thyrotoxicosis. Proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, chemosis, pretibial myxoedema and acropachy mean Graves' disease.
list.why: Fixes the most common viva mix-up.
list.no: Gemini's "eyes = Graves' only" was too broad: lid lag is not specific.

list.why: Eleven features in four groups of matching letters; much easier than one 11-letter word.
list.no: Present the 3 or 4 features that matter, not all 11.

list.why: Four positions, then the feel, then the nodes: three groups in the order you do them.
list.no: Chaperone and consent before you start. Never skip.
L: Arms by sides, hands on hips pressing in, arms up, leaning forward
Normal side first, every quadrant, axillary tail, nipple

list.code: Above and medial: inguinal. Below and lateral: femoral.
list.line: Relate the lump to the pubic tubercle. Controlled by pressure on the deep ring (midpoint of the inguinal ligament) means indirect.
list.why: One landmark rule decides the type.
list.no: Examine standing; many hernias reduce when lying.

list.line: Can you get above it (no = hernia)? Is it separate from the testis (epididymal cyst)? Does it transilluminate (fluid)?
list.why: Three yes or no questions that sort almost every scrotal lump.
list.no: A hard testicular lump is cancer until proven otherwise: 2-week-wait referral.

list.why: A memorable set where the letters all match, so you count to six.
list.no: Paraesthesia and paralysis are late and mean the limb is threatened: escalate, don't complete the list first.

list.line: Normal 0.9 to 1.3; under 0.8 no compression bandaging; under 0.5 critical; over 1.3 calcified, unreliable.
list.why: Four cut-offs tied to one decision each.
list.no: Highest ankle pressure divided by highest brachial pressure.

list.why: The universal joint sequence; the same five beats for knee, hip, shoulder and spine.
list.no: Ask about pain before you move anything, and watch their face.
L: Standing, walking, then on the couch: swelling, wasting, scars, alignment
Neurovascular status, joint above and below

list.code: Lachman for ACL, McMurray for meniscus, stress for collaterals
list.line: Lachman and anterior drawer: ACL. Posterior sag and drawer: PCL. Valgus and varus stress: MCL and LCL. McMurray: menisci.
list.why: Pairs each structure with its test.
list.no: In the station, say which structure each test checks as you do it.

list.line: Standing on the bad leg, the pelvis drops on the other (sound) side because the hip abductors are weak.
list.why: Three words for the most commonly reversed sign in MSK.
list.no: Thomas test is for fixed flexion; don't mix them.

list.why: Four letters in the order you examine.
list.no: Start with the 3 screening questions: pain or stiffness? dressing without difficulty? stairs without difficulty?

list.code: Right eye, right hand, right eye
list.line: Examine their right eye with your right hand and your right eye (and left with left). Red reflex first, then disc, vessels, background, macula last.
list.why: Fixes the most common practical error.
list.no: Dim the lights and ask them to look at a distant point.

list.line: Pull the pinna up and back in adults (down and back in children). Look at the good ear first.
list.why: One rule straightens the canal.
list.no: Use a new speculum for each ear.

list.line: Major (2 points each): change in size, shape, colour. Minor (1 point each): 7 mm or more, inflammation, oozing, change in sensation. Score 3 or more: suspected cancer referral.
list.why: NICE uses this score, so the numbers are the mark. ABCDE (asymmetry, border, colour, diameter, evolution) helps you look.
list.no: Any lesion the patient or doctor is worried about can still be referred.

list.why: Five groups in the order you work down and around the foot.
list.no: A hot, swollen foot with intact skin is Charcot foot until proven otherwise.
L: Ulcers, calluses, deformity, between the toes

list.why: The test is literally named after its four As.
list.no: Score 4 or more suggests delirium; it is a screen, not a diagnosis.
L: AMT4: age, date of birth, place, year
Attention: months of the year backwards

list.line: Under the chin, under the jaw, in front of the ear, behind the ear, back of the head; then down the front and back of the neck to above the collarbone.
list.why: A route around the head like a crown, then down: the body cues the next group.
list.no: Stand behind the patient and use both hands.

list.line: Lying for 5 minutes, then standing for 1 and 3 minutes. A drop of 20 systolic or 10 diastolic is postural hypotension.
list.why: Numbers that define the diagnosis are the mark.
list.no: Arm supported at heart level; cuff bladder covering most of the arm.

list.code: Chaperone, consent, left side, knees up
list.line: Then inspect, insert, and feel the prostate (size, surface, median sulcus, consistency, tenderness) and the rectal wall; check the glove.
list.why: The setup marks come before anything clinical.
list.no: Explain each step before you do it.

list.why: An unordered pile of objects on a tray: exactly what letters are best at. Set it up once and you never walk back to the trolley.
list.no: Keep the same letters for cannulation and only add to them (see TAGBS-P + CFD). Changing what a letter means between stations causes interference.
L: Sharps bin and a safety needle

list.code: Cultures, Clotting, Chemistry, Counts, Crossmatch, Glucose
list.line: Blood cultures, citrate (clotting), serum (U&E, LFT, CRP), heparin if used, EDTA (FBC, then crossmatch), fluoride (glucose).
list.why: Five Cs and a G in the order you fill. It's grouped by additive, so it holds whatever colours your trust uses.
list.no: Colours vary by maker (BD and Sarstedt differ). At NUH, LFT and CRP go in the gold or yellow serum tube, the one your friend called yellow.

list.line: Release the tourniquet before the needle comes out, then gauze and pressure.
list.why: The single most-failed venepuncture step, in three words.
list.no: Also: clean 30 seconds, dry 30 seconds, don't re-touch the vein.

list.code: Label at the bed, never away from it
list.line: Label each bottle in front of the patient, checking their details again; crossmatch is handwritten.
list.why: Wrong blood in tube is a never-event; the rhyme makes the location the cue.
list.no: Don't pre-label bottles.

list.why: Same tray plus three: you reuse a memory you already own instead of learning a new code.
list.no: Advance 2 mm after flashback, then slide the cannula off the needle.
L: Cannula: smallest gauge that works (pink 20G routine)

list.why: Three steps that mirror each other.
list.no: Five rights before you start: patient, drug, dose, route, time.

list.code: Allen's: colour back in 5 to 15 s
list.line: Press both arteries, fist, open, release the ulnar: colour should return within 5 to 15 seconds. Heparinised syringe, 45°, firm pressure 3 to 5 minutes (longer if anticoagulated), analyse within 10 minutes.
list.why: The numbers are the decisions in this procedure.
list.no: Gemini's "ALLEN-5" was contrived and said under 5 seconds; most teaching uses 5 to 15.

list.why: The letters are the measuring route on the body, and the number is the safety check (NHS patient safety alert).
list.no: Never use the "whoosh" test.
L: Aspirate pH 5.5 or below before anything goes down; if not, X-ray

list.code: Urine before balloon; foreskin back before you go
list.line: Lidocaine gel and wait 3 to 5 minutes; advance until urine flows (to the hilt in men); then inflate the balloon with sterile water to the stated volume; replace the foreskin.
list.why: Two safety rules in one rhyme: a balloon in the urethra and paraphimosis are the serious harms.
list.no: Gemini's "ANTT-2G-SLB" can't be said aloud, so it fails as a mnemonic. And the drug is lidocaine (UK name), not lignocaine.

list.code: Stretch for IM, pinch for SC
list.line: Intramuscular: 90°, skin stretched, no need to aspirate (Green Book). Subcutaneous: skin bunched, 45° (or 90° with short pen needles).
list.why: One contrast for both stations.
list.no: Gemini's "Z-DARTS" said aspirate and wait 15 to 30 minutes. The Green Book says aspiration isn't needed and finds no evidence for longer observation.

list.line: For local anaesthetic infiltration, aspirate to avoid a vein. Lidocaine maximum about 3 mg/kg plain, 7 mg/kg with adrenaline.
list.why: The opposite of IM vaccines, which is exactly why it needs its own rule.
list.no: Check allergy and the maximum dose before you draw up.

list.line: Clockwise from the right arm: Red, Yellow, Green, Black. Chest: V1 and V2 at the 4th space either side of the sternum, V4 5th space midclavicular, V3 between, V5 and V6 level with V4 at the anterior and mid axillary lines.
list.why: A phrase whose first letters are the colours, in the order you go round the body.
list.no: US colours differ; the UK uses this one.

list.code: Stand, zero, seal, blast: best of 3
list.line: Stand up, set the pointer to zero, deep breath, lips sealed, short sharp blast; record the best of 3.
list.why: A rhythm you can say while doing it.
list.no: Compare with their best or predicted value, not a single number.

list.code: MDI slow and steady; dry powder quick and deep
list.line: MDI: shake, breathe out, seal, press as you start a slow breath in, hold 10 seconds. Dry powder: no shake, breathe in fast and hard.
list.why: The contrast is the commonest error, so it gets the rhyme.
list.no: A spacer helps with MDIs; check technique at every review.

list.code: Ask, don't tell; obs at 0, 15 and the end
list.line: Ask the patient to say their name and date of birth; match wristband, prescription and blood label; check expiry and special requirements. Observations before, 15 minutes in, and within an hour of finishing.
list.why: Positive identification plus three timed sets of observations.
list.no: Never ask "Are you John Smith?"; anyone can say yes.

list.line: A single parameter scoring 3, or a total of 5 or more: urgent review. Total 7 or more: emergency. New confusion scores 3 on its own.
list.why: Three numbers decide the escalation.
list.no: Use SpO2 scale 2 only for documented hypercapnic respiratory failure.

list.why: Five verbs in the order your hands move.
list.no: Check the rate twice; a decimal slip is a serious error.
L: Prescription, patient, fluid, expiry, bag intact
Spike the bag without touching key parts

list.line: Clean, dry hands; prick the side of the fingertip, not the pad; apply the drop to the strip.
list.why: One rule prevents the commonest discomfort mistake.
list.no: Check the meter's quality control and strip expiry.

list.code: Over 65? Don't dip for a UTI
list.line: Nitrites plus leucocytes suggest infection in younger adults; in over-65s a dipstick can't diagnose a UTI.
list.why: The national guidance most often missed.
list.no: Read each pad at its stated time.

list.line: Water runs from clean (fingertips) to less clean (elbows); keep hands above the elbows and in front of you.
list.why: One rule explains every step.
list.no: Closed gloving: hands stay inside the sleeves.

list.line: Explain, consent, correct swab and medium, rotate over the area, label, send.
list.why: A short, logical sequence you understand. A mnemonic would add a decoding step and nothing else.
list.no: This is an example of when not to mnemonicify.

list.line: Aseptic non-touch technique: key parts never touch; clean from the wound outwards; date the dressing.
list.why: The principle (ANTT) does the work; there is no list to hold.
list.no: Understanding beats letters here.

primer.t: When a mnemonic helps, and when it hurts
pts: Best for 3 to 7 separate items with no natural order: equipment trays, symptom screens. A 2019 study found an acronym helped people learn a procedure's steps.
Best for anything done on the body in sequence. The body cues the next stop. The method of loci gave a medium-sized recall boost in a 2021 meta-analysis.
Best for the one step you must never get backwards (off before out) and for contrasts (mood is climate, affect is weather). Nothing to decode.
Best for thresholds and timings, paired with the decision each number makes.
Best for long lists: split into 3 or 4 meaningful groups rather than one 10-letter word.
Skip it when the plain words are the mark (capacity), or the steps follow from understanding (wound care). Too many look-alike codes interfere with each other.
